newsitem.title: UK: OPEC oil output over quota again, easily absorbed.
newsitem.headline: OPEC oil output over quota again, easily absorbed.

text.p: OPEC oil producers continued to flout their own output quotas in August but the market is easily absorbing the extra oil at much higher prices than forecast earlier.

Market analysts say the crisis in Iraq has put on hold the return of Iraqi oil exports and probably means the market will be short of about 650,000 barrels per day (bpd) of additional oil which it had expected, beginning this month.
The loss of the Iraqi exports comes when demand is robust, production from rival producers is lower than forecast and inventories of heating fuel are thin heading into the Northern Hemisphere winter.
"Demand is so strong and stocks are low. So the market really does need that extra Iraqi oil now," said Leo Drollas, chief economist at the Centre for Global Energy Studies (CGES), on Thursday.

A Reuter survey of oil analysts, industry officials and OPEC delegates showed that OPEC members pumped 25.88 million barrels per day (bpd) in August, up 20,000 bpd from 25.86 million in July and well over their 25.03 million bpd ceiling.

"OPEC has been overproducing for a long time but that overproduction becomes a problem only when demand is lower than supply. Now it is not a problem," sad Bo Van Wijk, vice president of energy risk managment at Swiss bank UBS.

Baghdad's recent attacks on Kurdish strongholds sparked retaliatory U.S. missile attacks and prompted an indefinite delay in the implementation of a U.N. pact allowing Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil to pay for food and medical supplies.
Oil prices currently stand about $5 a barrel above levels seen this time last year, defying oil pundits' predictions of weaker oil prices when the oil-for-food deal was signed in May.
The OPEC reference basket hit $21.17 on Wednesday, nearly $2 above early August levels and above its $21 "minimum" target.

The CGES, a London energy think-tank headed by former Saudi oil minister Sheikh Ahmed Zaki Yamani, reckons OPEC producers stand to earn $2 billion more in the fourth quarter than was previously forecast.
"OPEC has had a very good ride this quarter and things look better for the fourth quarter. We have seen a dramatic change in market sentiment," Drollas said.
Since producers' revenues have exceeded even the most optimistic predictions, analysts say there is little incentive for the more wayward OPEC members to rein in overproduction.
"With these kind of prices and given the strong demand, OPEC is wise to let the market have a few more barrels quietly," Van Wijk said.
Virtually every OPEC member is over its production quota but some, namely Middle East Gulf producers only modestly so.

According to the Reuter survey, higher production in August was recorded in three of OPEC's largest members -- Venezuela, Nigeria and Iran. Venezuela pumped out 3.12 million bpd, up from 3.03 million in July and well above its 2.36 million quota.
Despite official denials, Venezuelan oil industry sources say output surged to 3.3 million bpd in mid-August and is on target to average 3.2 million bpd this month.
"It is unclear how much production will come up by year's end but they were able to do 3.3 million two weeks ago," one Latin American oil industry source said.
The group's other main overproducer, Nigeria, has fully recovered from a midsummer supply shortfall in the giant Bonny system because of pipeline leaks.
Sources at one Nigerian equity producer said his company was told by Abuja to produce "flat out" in August and September.
"It would appear Nigeria was unconcerned about (OPEC) quotas for the next few months," the source said.
OPEC's largest member, Saudi Arabia, has not provided its official August output figures but analysts estimate it produced around 8.10 million bpd, below July's 8.22 million.
Saudi sources said the kingdom's supply to the market complied with its 8.0 million bpd OPEC quota.
Moreover, industry sources point out the kingdom's exports are to be cut five percent in both August and September because of higher than expected summer demand for oil in the country.
